newsitem.title: USA: U.S. space shuttle landing delayed.
newsitem.headline: U.S. space shuttle landing delayed.

text.p: Cloudy skies in Florida delayed the homecoming on Saturday of the space shuttle Atlantis with former Mir resident Jerry Linenger.

Atlantis was due to land at the Kennedy Space Centre at 7:52 a.m. EDT (1152 GMT), but low clouds over the shuttle's three-mile (5-km) long runway forced flight controllers to postpone the landing for at least 90 minutes, mission control commentator Kyle Herring said.
"The first landing opportunity is not going to be possible," Herring said. Atlantis's landing was tentatively rescheduled for on orbit later, at 9:27 a.m. EDT (1327 GMT).
NASA officials had said they would not divert the shuttle to its backup landing strip at Edwards Air Force Base in California.
If the weather did not cooperate, conditions in Florida looked much better on Sunday, flight director Wayne Hale said on Friday.
The shuttle's seven-member crew had earlier packed up their gear and closed the spaceship's clam-like cargo bay doors in preparation for landing.

Linenger, the fourth NASA astronaut to live and work aboard Mir, was to ride home in a cushioned reclining seat on the shuttle's lower deck. His four-month stay on Mir was marred by a serious fire, life support problems and a near collision with an unmanned cargo craft.
The 42-year-old medical doctor and navy captain said he was determined to walk off the shuttle after its landing, despite NASA's preference for him to be carried off.

During his stay on Mir, Linenger, who lists marathon running and ocean swimming as hobbies, was to run daily for two hours on a treadmill to keep up his strength. Although that exercise programme was disrupted by Mir's problems, NASA did not expect any complications after Linenger's return.
Long-duration space flights, away from the pull of gravity, cause bones to weaken and muscles to waste away.

If the shuttle lands as planned, Linenger will have spent 132 days in space, the second-longest mission for an American astronaut. Shannon Lucid set the current U.S. record with a 188-day stay on Mir last year.
Linenger said it would be "pure elation" to be reunited with his 18-month old son, John, and his wife, Kathryn, who is expecting their second child in June.
